When you think about sentence stress in English, you have to distinguish between content words and function words. These two types of words have different stress in a sentence.
In a conversation, the listener subconsciously listens to the content words in a sentence, getting the main idea of what is being said.

In sentences there are content words, which are usually nouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs. These are words bring images to mind to tell us where to. To help the listener grasp the main content of the story, you use stress and intonation with content words to bring attention to them.

There are also function words, which help structure sentences. These can be pronouns, determiners, prepositions, or auxiliary. When function words are missing or used incorrectly, the listener can probably still get the main idea. Since function words don't give content, they don't need added attention or stress.

Personal pronouns are function words - they do not provide any real content. Rather, they help to structure the sentence grammatically. Therefore, you do not usually place any stress on them when you read a sentence.

For example (bolded words are stressed):
I like them.
When you pronounce the word like, your voice should be slightly louder and higher in pitch than the function words (I, them).
Depending on the what the speaker is trying to convey, it is possible to stress some function words.

For example:
I like him, not her.
In this context, the speaker wants to be very clear to the listener about who they like.

images.text: With society becoming more individualistic, many people are starting to discover the beauty in being truly kind to those around them. Good social etiquette requires that we remain polite and respectful to everyone. Yet, we are sometimes surprised by simple actions that are out of the ordinary or completely unexpected. We may never know who initiated an action and it may be impossible to give thanks, making the gesture even more “random” or arbitrary. These actions are sometimes called “random acts of kindness” and they remind us that altruism does exist.

American author Anne Herbert is credited with first coining the term “random act of kindness” when she wrote the phrase: “practice random kindness and senseless acts of beauty” on a placemat in 1982. She later published a book entitled “Random Acts of Kindness”.
Many people have their own idea of what a random act of kindness looks like. I've come up with a few suggestions:
When you are finished reading it, leave a magazine or newspaper in a place someone else can find it. It is the perfect way to reuse something.
Remember to be sincerely respectful of others when you are on the internet, as you would if you were speaking to them in person. Say hello, and leave a chat with “goodbye”.

At some point in time, we've all had to call the handyman to help us out. The kitchen sink backs up, or a leaky faucet gets worse; a window needs to be reinforced or the furnace needs replacing. The next time someone is at your house fixing something, offer them a drink or a snack. Let them know you truly appreciate the work they are doing for you.
You're in a long lineup at the airport. You're not going to miss your flight, but someone behind you in line might. Let them move ahead. Also, if waiting in the line seems to be more difficult for some people because of their age or because they are travelling with young children, let them go ahead of you. They will remember how you helped them out.
